_comment: Soft-tissue and drainage steps. Shared by abscess drainage, wound debridement and minor procedures.

step.st.local.title: Local anaesthesia for an inflamed field
step.st.local.why: Local anaesthetic works poorly in the acidic tissue of an abscess, which is why patients remember these procedures. Say so, and plan around it.
how: Infiltrate a field block in healthy tissue around the abscess rather than into it.
Check the maximum safe dose for the patient's weight and whether adrenaline is appropriate for that site.
If adequate anaesthesia cannot be achieved, stop and do it under general anaesthesia rather than doing it badly.
pitfalls: Injecting into the cavity, which hurts and does not work.
Exceeding the maximum dose when a large area needs infiltration.

step.st.incision.title: Incision over the collection
step.st.incision.why: The incision must be long enough and placed so the cavity drains with gravity, or the abscess reforms and the patient returns.
how: Incise at the point of maximal fluctuance, along skin tension lines where cosmesis matters, and at the most dependent point where drainage matters.
Make the incision long enough to allow the cavity to be explored and to keep draining as it heals.
For a pilonidal abscess, drain off the midline.
structuresAtRisk: Facial nerve branches in a parotid or facial abscess
Anal sphincter complex in a perianal abscess
pitfalls: A stab incision that closes over within a day.
An incision placed for convenience rather than for dependent drainage.

step.st.culture.title: Pus for culture
step.st.culture.why: Pus obtained at drainage is the specimen that guides therapy. A superficial swab of intact skin taken afterwards answers a different and less useful question.
how: Aspirate or swab pus from within the cavity at the moment it is opened, before irrigation.
Send in an appropriate container, and request anaerobic culture where the site suggests it.
Record on the request what the patient has already had, so the laboratory can interpret a negative culture.
pitfalls: Sending no culture from an abscess in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient.

step.st.deloculate.title: Breaking down loculations
step.st.deloculate.why: An abscess that is not fully de-loculated is an abscess that has been partly drained, and it is the commonest reason for recurrence and readmission.
how: Explore the whole cavity with a finger or a blunt instrument and break every septum.
Feel for the extent in every direction, particularly deep, where the cavity is usually larger than the skin suggests.
For a perianal abscess, consider examination under anaesthesia to exclude ischiorectal, supralevator or horseshoe extension.
structuresAtRisk: Named vessels and nerves at the base of a deep cavity
pitfalls: Stopping at the first gush of pus.
Probing forcibly through the cavity wall and creating a false passage.

step.st.debride.title: Debridement of non-viable tissue
step.st.debride.why: Antibiotics do not reach dead tissue. In necrotising infection the extent of debridement at the first operation is the strongest determinant of survival.
how: Excise to bleeding, contractile, healthy tissue in every direction.
In necrotising infection, follow the plane of easy finger dissection: where the fascia separates without resistance, the disease has been.
Plan a re-look at 24 to 48 hours as the default, not as a rescue.
structuresAtRisk: Named neurovascular structures at the margin of debridement
Viable skin that will be needed for later closure
pitfalls: A conservative first debridement in necrotising infection.
Debriding to a cosmetic margin rather than a physiological one.

step.st.pack.title: Irrigation, packing and leaving the wound open
step.st.pack.why: An abscess cavity closed primarily becomes an abscess again. It is left open, or lightly packed, so it heals from the base up.
how: Irrigate with saline until the effluent is clear.
Pack lightly if at all: the purpose is to keep the skin edges apart, not to fill the cavity under pressure.
Arrange the first dressing change and tell the patient who will do it and when.
pitfalls: Tight packing, which causes pain and pressure necrosis.
Discharging a patient with a packed wound and no dressing plan.
